new_statements.quote: At the suprasegmental level, Dh. is a fairly "classical" pitch-accent language of East Africa — but note that many monosyllables contrast for the presence/absence of accent, and that absence of accent seems on the whole far more common that its presence.
new_statements.citation: Tosco, Mauro. 2001. The Dhaasanac Language: Grammar, Texts, Vocabulary of a Cushitic Language of Ethiopia. (Kuschitische Sprachstudien 17.) Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.
new_statements.locator: p. 11, §1.2.2 'Grammatical profile' (publisher sample PDF page 25; verified against page image)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (29-page Köppe publisher sample). extracted text of PDF page 25 and a rendered page image (110 dpi) both show printed p. 11, §1.2.2 'Grammatical profile', with the sentence exactly as quoted: 'At the suprasegmental level, Dh. is a fairly "classical" pitch accent language of East Africa — but note that many monosyllables contrast for the presence/absence of accent, and that absence of accent seems on the whole far more common that its presence.' (print typo 'that' for 'than' is real; the only glyph difference is the book's dash rendering in 'pitch–accent'). Surrounding section: it is the author's typological summary of the phonology; the TOC (sample p. v) confirms §2.2 Accent and tone…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dhaasanac is described as a pitch accent language: a word carries at most one (high-pitch) accent whose presence or absence is lexically distinctive (minimal pairs even among monosyllables), and most words are unaccented. The book's TOC has a dedicated §2.2.3 'Accent placement' (pp. 38-42) and §2.3.7 'Intonation and stress' (pp. 55-60), so a placement rule exists in the full grammar, but those pages are not in the open sample; the accessible statement establishes the system type, not the position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the accessible pages.
new_statements.exceptions: Many monosyllables contrast for presence vs absence of accent; absence of accent is the more common case. Mous (2012: §4.2; 2022) reports from Tosco 2001: 36 that the tone-bearing unit is the mora.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical accent (grammatical-profile statement); the grammar separately treats 'Intonation and stress' at §2.3.7, implying 'stress' is distinguished from the lexical pitch accent, but that section was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Tosco 2001 describes Dhaasanac as spoken by the Dhaasanac of the Omo delta, SW Ethiopia (fieldwork 1998, main informant Moses Nanok Yierg'alle); Sasse 1974/1976 call the same language Galab/Dasenech and note undelimited internal dialect variation. All map to daas1238 (no separate dialect glottocodes involved).

sources.note: p. 11 (Grammatical profile): Dhaasanac is 'a fairly "classical" pitch accent language of East Africa', with many monosyllables contrasting presence vs absence of accent and absence of accent far more common than presence. TOC shows §2.2 Accent and tone (34), 2.2.1 Falling and rising pitch contours (36), 2.2.2 Tonal minimal pairs (37), 2.2.3 Accent placement (38-42), §2.3.1 The mora (42), §2.3.7 Intonation and stress (55-60) — those pages are not in the sample. p. 7: in the BTL/Wycliffe orthography 'Tone is marked, it seems, when necessary for purposes of disambiguation.'

East Lansing: African Studies Center, Michigan State University. — Rosetta Project excerpt (pp. 196-199 intro + 2.1 Segmental phonology; pp. 215-217 comparative phonology; morphosyntax pages)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Excerpted phonology section (2.1) is segmental only; the only accent remark is p. 199: 'Unaccented final i and u are lowered to [e] and [o], resp.' Acute accent marks (e.g. tákac 'one', kósol 'laugh!') are used in transcription but no placement statement appears in the excerpted pages; refers to Sasse 1974 for 'low-level rules'.
Segmental inventory only; notes orthographic acute and circumflex accents on vowels; no statement on stress or accent placement.
